Volume 15 · Chapter 09

Environmental, energy and climate economics

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v15-c08

By the endEvaluate externalities and long-horizon choices under uncertainty.

Environmental, energy and climate economics

The difficult environmental decision is rarely whether pollution is undesirable. It is how much prevention to buy, when to buy it, who should pay, and which uncertainty the policy should absorb. A cheap electricity bill can conceal uncompensated damage; a large tax receipt can coexist with a small real resource saving. This chapter builds five complete economies that keep those distinctions visible.

Capability. Derive efficient emissions and resource paths, compare price and quantity instruments under a stated information structure, value risky protection using marginal utility, and reconcile energy investment with household and government accounts. Prerequisites are convex optimization, expected utility, present value and the distinction between behavioral evidence and welfare criteria developed in the preceding chapter. All quantities below are synthetic. No number estimates actual climate damages, emissions, carbon prices or policy effects.

Consumption is the numeraire. An emissions unit is an abstract physical unit; a tax has units of consumption per emissions unit. Damage functions measure lost consumption equivalents, not tax payments. Benefits, costs and probabilities are stipulated primitives. Aggregate surplus uses equal marginal social weights on consumption except in the explicitly specified expected-utility case. Changing distributional weights changes the planner problem; identifying preferences experimentally does not by itself choose those weights.

1. Externality correction and the distribution of receipts

Let emitter i have baseline emissions bᵢ, abatement aᵢ between zero and bᵢ, and convex resource cost Cᵢ(aᵢ). Total remaining emissions are E=Σ(bᵢ−aᵢ). With increasing convex damage D(E), the planner minimizes L=ΣCᵢ(aᵢ)+D(E). A compact feasible box and continuity give existence. Strictly convex abatement costs make L strictly convex, so a feasible point satisfying the first-order inequalities is the unique global minimum.

The derivative is Cᵢ′(aᵢ)−D′(E). At an interior optimum it is zero; at aᵢ=0 it must be nonnegative; at aᵢ=bᵢ it must be nonpositive. To prove sufficiency, convexity gives L(a)−L(a*)≥∇L(a*)·(a−a*). Each term on the right is nonnegative using its boundary sign. This proof handles saturated emitters without pretending their marginal costs must equal those of interior emitters.

A uniform emissions tax τ=D′(E*) implements this solution when each emitter minimizes Cᵢ(aᵢ)+τ(bᵢ−aᵢ), takes τ as given, and expects no action-dependent refund. A tradable aggregate cap E* implements the same cost-minimizing allocation at permit price τ, with competitive permit trade and the same technological assumptions. Equal marginal abatement costs establish cost effectiveness at a specified cap; they do not establish that the cap itself is socially optimal. Enforcement, output responses, preexisting distortions and market power are absent here.

Worked case 1: an efficient tax with explicit household accounts

Two households each own one emitter. Each receives baseline operating resources 60. The primitives are (6,6,1,2,1/2,60): b₁=b₂=6, Cᵢ=kᵢaᵢ²/2 with k=(1,2), and D(E)=E²/4, so its marginal slope is 1/2. Each household suffers half the damage. Output is fixed, abatement uses real goods, taxes are paid from operating resources, and government rebates the receipts equally.

Write λ=E/2. Interior conditions give a₁=λ, a₂=λ/2 and E=12−3λ/2. Therefore (a₁,a₂,E,τ)=(24/7,12/7,48/7,24/7). Both abatements lie strictly between zero and six, validating the branch. Real abatement costs are 288/49 and 144/49; damage is 576/49. Thus (abatement cost,damage,total loss,gain)=(432/49,576/49,144/7,108/7), where the gain compares with unregulated damage 36.

Taxes on remaining emissions are 432/49 and 720/49. Total receipts are 1152/49 and each rebate is 576/49. Net household utility, including damage, is (U₁,U₂)=(2508/49,2364/49), versus 42 each without policy. Adding the two budgets cancels tax payments against rebates and leaves 120 minus real abatement costs and damage. Positive receipts are therefore not an additional social benefit. All payments fit inside the stipulated operating resources.

Auctioning 48/7 permits generates the same receipts. Giving each household a fixed entitlement of 24/7 permits produces the same wealth transfer at this price: its permit endowment is worth 576/49. A freely allocated permit still has an opportunity cost when used. Equivalence requires fixed entitlements; grants conditional on current output or abatement change incentives. Distribution can also change without changing efficient emissions, as Exercise 2 demonstrates.

2. Which uncertainty should an instrument absorb?

Commitment precedes learning. Government chooses a fixed tax or cap, then the firm observes its cost shock and chooses abatement. Government cannot condition policy on the realized shock. This information restriction matters: with observable costs and state-contingent instruments, the following comparison would be a different problem. Assume an interior quadratic environment: baseline emissions B, cost Cθ(a)=(c₀+θ)a+ka²/2 and damage d(B−a)²/2, where k,d>0 and Eθ=0. Restrict shocks so costs remain increasing and all choices discussed stay in [0,B].

The full-information optimum is a*(θ)=(dB−c₀−θ)/(k+d). Put ā=(dB−c₀)/(k+d). The fixed cap requires a=ā; the fixed tax τ=d(B−ā) induces a=ā−θ/k. Completing the square in total cost yields exactly Lθ(a)−Lθ(a*)=(k+d)(a−a*)²/2. Hence expected regret is Var(θ)/[2(k+d)] for the cap and d²Var(θ)/[2k²(k+d)] for the tax. Their ratio is (d/k)². These are global comparisons for these two fixed instruments in this interior quadratic model, not universal rankings of environmental regulation.

The mechanism is responsiveness. With a tax, high costs reduce abatement. That flexibility saves resources but changes damage. When marginal damage rises sharply relative to marginal cost, the emissions error is expensive and the cap wins. The slope statement concerns cost uncertainty with this timing. Uncertain damage that firms do not respond to need not create any difference in behavior. The MIT instrument-choice lecture supplies the method context; the exact finite example and proof here are original.

Worked case 2: binary cost risk

Take (B,c₀,k,d,θlow,θhigh,p)=(10,2,2,1,-1,1,1/2). Mean-calibrated abatement is 8/3 and the tax is 22/3. Full-information abatement is 3 in the low-cost state and 7/3 in the high-cost state. The tax induces 19/6 and 13/6; the cap keeps abatement at 8/3 in both. Each choice is feasible and interior.

The resulting comparison is (cap regret,tax regret)=(1/6,1/24). Direct evaluation also gives (full information,cap,tax)=(235/6,118/3,941/24). Tax losses by state are 877/24 and 1005/24. These include abatement resources and damage; tax payments are transfers to government and are rebated state by state. Assume an initial operating endowment of 200 for the emitter so that each realized tax and abatement bill can be paid without borrowing.

This comparison isolates one reason for instrument choice. It omits permit banking, tax adjustment, enforcement risk, nonlinear catastrophes and political commitment failure. A finding that the tax wins here does not establish that actual marginal climate damage has this slope. Estimating physical damage and reporting uncertainty about it is a distinct empirical task.

3. Risk, welfare weights and long horizons

A discount factor is not merely a number selected from a finance table. For social objective u(C₀)+βΣpₛu(C₁ₛ), a small project costing one unit now and yielding Xₛ later has marginal net value −1+ΣpₛmₛXₛ in current consumption units, where mₛ=βu′(C₁ₛ)/u′(C₀). Derive this by differentiating utility in project scale and dividing by positive u′(C₀). These are social marginal valuations. They become traded security prices only under additional household opportunity and market-clearing conditions, which are not imposed here.

The identity E[mX]=E[m]E[X]+Cov(m,X) separates timing from state dependence. Protection paying in low-consumption states can be more valuable even with the same expected physical benefit. Applying a risk premium to the payoff and then again to the discount factor can count risk twice. Nor is a baseline marginal value sufficient to evaluate a large project: as scale changes consumption, the marginal valuation changes too.

Worked case 3: protection in a bad state or a good state

The primitives are (C₀,Cbad,Cgood,β,p,k,benefit)=(100,50,150,9/10,1/2,9,20). Project scale x∈[0,1] costs kx now. Project A avoids loss 20x only in the bad state; B avoids loss 20x only in the good state. These are alternative technologies, evaluated separately. Log utility is defined throughout the feasible interval. Benefits are physical avoided consumption losses, not cash created by an unfunded promise.

Baseline discount factors and values are (mbad,mgood,value A,value B,safe value)=(9/5,3/5,18,6,6/5). Both expected benefits are 10, but multiplying each by the average factor gives 12 and misses their different covariance. A safe marginal unit has value 6/5; its reciprocal 5/6 is a shadow gross return, not a claimed market bond rate.

For A, utility is log(100−9x)+(9/20)log(50+20x)+(9/20)log150. Its derivative is −9/(100−9x)+9/(50+20x), positive through x=1; the zero would be 50/29 outside the feasible interval. Strict concavity then proves xA=1 globally. B replaces 50+20x with 150+20x in the corresponding first-derivative term; its first derivative is negative throughout, so xB=0. The full-scale utility changes are (ΔUA,ΔUB)=(0.0571018270083,-0.0379872651419). Exact expressions are log(91/100)+(9/20)log(7/5) and log(91/100)+(9/20)log(17/15). This establishes finite decisions directly rather than extrapolating the marginal ranking.

For deterministic consumption growth Cₜ=C₀(1+g)ᵗ and constant-relative-risk-aversion marginal utility C⁻η, the time-zero marginal factor is mₜ=[β/(1+g)η]t. Equivalently write R=(1+g)η/β and mₜ=R⁻ᵗ. The exact expression precedes the approximate annual-rate formula often used in discussion. β expresses pure time preference, η curvature and inequality aversion in this representative-consumption aggregation, and g the assumed consumption path. They are not interchangeable parameters. Unknown future growth requires an expectation of marginal utility, not automatic substitution of expected growth into this nonlinear formula.

Social discounting also requires specifying whose consumption is counted. A representative global aggregate can conceal losses concentrated among poorer populations. A distribution-sensitive analysis uses group-specific marginal welfare weights and an explicit aggregation rule. Empirical damage functions, adaptation, nonmarket losses and ethical weights should be reported separately. The finite consumption-pricing discussion in QuantEcon's asset-pricing chapter provides the reused marginal-utility foundation; the welfare criteria and synthetic projects here are stipulated, not empirical estimates.

4. Exhaustible stocks: scarcity is an opportunity cost

An exhaustible resource couples dates even without pollution. Extracting today removes a future option. Consider two dates with a stock constraint q₀+q₁≤S, qₜ≥0, gross benefits B₀(q)=12q−q²/2 and B₁(q)=14q−q²/2, unit extraction cost 2 and discount factor β=4/5. Net social surplus is W=10q₀−q₀²/2+β(12q₁−q₁²/2). Strict concavity and compact feasibility give a unique allocation. At S=0 the allocation is trivially zero. For positive S, multiplier λ≥0 satisfies 10−q₀≤λ and β(12−q₁)≤λ, with equality for positive extraction and λ(S−q₀−q₁)=0.

These conditions are sufficient: the concave tangent bounds any alternative's welfare gain by λ times the change in total extraction plus nonpositive contributions from inactive dates. Feasibility and complementary slackness make that bound nonpositive. Solving gives three regimes. For 0<S≤2/5, q₀=S,q₁=0,λ=10−S. For 2/5≤S≤22, q₀=(4S+2)/9,q₁=(5S−2)/9,λ=4(22−S)/9. For S≥22, q₀=10,q₁=12,λ=0 and the excess stock is left underground. Formulas agree at both thresholds; thus stock exhaustion is a result only when scarcity binds.

Competitive inverse demands p₀=12−q₀ and p₁=14−q₁ support these allocations. A price-taking resource owner maximizes discounted receipts net of extraction costs subject to its stock. With positive extraction at both dates, p₁−2=(p₀−2)/β: the net scarcity rent grows at the gross discount rate. The gross price need not. When extraction is zero at a date, the corresponding inequality replaces the equality. Hunt Allcott's MIT resource-economics notes provide the resource-allocation method; our boundary-complete numerical economy is independently derived.

Worked case 4: an eight-unit deposit

Set (S,β,c,a₀,a₁)=(8,4/5,2,12,14). The allocation and prices are (q₀,q₁,p₀,p₁,λ)=(34/9,38/9,74/9,88/9,56/9). Net rents are 56/9 and 70/9; their ratio is 5/4. The stock is fully exhausted, and its present-value rent is λS=448/9.

Consumers have 100 units of numeraire at each date and quasilinear utility Bₜ(q)+n; the resource owner receives sale proceeds and pays the real extraction cost. At displayed prices consumer bills fit within their date-specific endowments. Their numeraire is 100−pₜqₜ, owner net consumption is (pₜ−2)qₜ, and aggregate numeraire is 100−2qₜ. Thus transfers reconcile without a missing counterparty. The owner and social calculation use the same stipulated present-value weight β; no unmodeled intertemporal trading market is asserted.

Discounted consumer surplus is q₀²/2+βq₁²/2=214/15. Adding resource-owner rent gives (consumer surplus,rent,welfare)=(214/15,448/9,2882/45), equal to direct evaluation of W. A tax changes the owner’s net rent path; physical scarcity alone does not make the competitive allocation climate efficient when emissions cause an omitted externality.

5. Capacity, dispatch and persistent damages

Energy investment is made before weather is known, whereas dispatch occurs afterward. Those are different margins. We model a utility under a cost-pass-through contract, not a merchant electricity market. Load is fixed at ten units in each of two equiprobable weather states, with gross consumption value 200. Existing thermal capacity of ten is sunk and sufficient for reliability. New renewable capacity K∈[0,20] costs cK in current goods. Availability a is one or one-half. Renewable production is min(10,aK), with costless curtailment; thermal production is G=max(10−aK,0). Thermal operating resources cost five per unit, and each thermal unit emits one unit.

Expected thermal use is 10−3K/4 on [0,10] and 5−K/4 on [10,20]. If its relevant running cost is h, total cost J=cK+hE[G] has slopes c−3h/4 and c−h/4. Since the second slope is larger, this piecewise-linear objective is convex. Its global minimizers are: K=0 if c>3h/4; every K∈[0,10] at equality; K=10 if h/4<c<3h/4; every K∈[10,20] if c=h/4; and K=20 if c<h/4. Comparing slopes proves the entire correspondence, including ties, rather than selecting one arbitrary corner.

Worked case 5: a funded transition to renewable capacity

Take (load,availability₁,availability₂,p,c,thermal cost,damage)=(10,1,1/2,1/2,4,5,2). Discounting between investment and operation is one by assumption. Damage is two consumption units per emissions unit, borne by the same consumers; this is a synthetic reduced-form damage value. The untaxed utility uses h=5, so both slopes are positive and K=0. The social planner uses h=7, giving slopes −5/4 and 9/4, hence K=10.

A carbon charge of two induces the utility to use h=7. At K=10 thermal generation is zero or five, while renewable production is ten or five. Load clears in each state. The comparison is (private K,social K,unregulated social cost,regulated social cost,gain)=(0,10,70,115/2,25/2). The regulated cost is capital 40, expected thermal resources 25/2, and expected damage five.

Consumers own 100 current and 100 future numeraire units. A current bill of 40 fully finances construction. The operating bill is zero in good weather and 35 in poor weather, paid out of future resources; government refunds the associated carbon receipts of zero or ten to these consumers in the same state. No expected revenue is borrowed to cover a bad-state shortfall. The expected bill including capital is 115/2, the expected rebate five, and net resource expense 105/2; adding damage five restores social cost 115/2. Thus (expected tax,bill,net bill,damage)=(5,115/2,105/2,5). Welfare is fixed load value minus social cost; the charge changes incentives but is not itself a resource cost.

A constant damage charge can summarize a longer stock mechanism only under appropriate assumptions. Let a pollutant stock satisfy Sₜ₊₁=ρSₜ+eₜ, with 0≤ρ≤1 and damages Dⱼ(Sⱼ) at dates j through a finite terminal date T. A marginal emissions pulse at t changes stock at j by ρj−t−1. If mⱼ is the time-zero consumption discount factor and damages are differentiable, its date-t marginal damage is Σⱼ₌ₜ₊₁ᵀ(mⱼ/mₜ)Dⱼ′(Sⱼ)ρj−t−1. This follows by differentiating the stock recurrence, then applying the chain rule to discounted damages. There is no second discount factor to multiply into this expression.

With uncertainty, the date-zero version is E[ΣmⱼDⱼ′(Sⱼ)∂Sⱼ/∂e₀]; covariance between consumption, damages and persistence belongs inside the expectation. Nonlinear damages, changing adaptation and multiple gases require a richer state model. Neither a single decay parameter nor a constant per-unit damage estimate is asserted to describe the actual climate system. The useful discipline is to show physical response, marginal damage, welfare weights and discounting separately.

Exercises

  1. In case 1 impose an aggregate emissions cap of two. Find the cost-minimizing abatements, permit price, real abatement cost, damage and auction receipts. Prove the global solution with its binding individual limit. Is this the welfare-optimal cap?
  2. Keep the efficient tax in case 1 but give all receipts to household 2. Compute both utilities, compare each with no policy, and find the minimum transfer from 2 to 1 that makes 1 whole. Explain why aggregate gains alone do not establish a Pareto improvement.
  3. Change case 2 to d=4, keeping its cost shock and all other primitives. Derive the cap, tax, full-information choices and both expected regrets. Check all choices are interior and give the instrument ranking.
  4. Instead remove cost uncertainty (θ=0) and let d be one or three with equal probabilities, learned after policy commitment. Calibrate the cap and tax at mean d=2. Do their realized abatement choices differ? Compute their common expected total cost and expected regret relative to full information. State why the cost-shock rule cannot simply be reused.
  5. In case 3 change project unit cost to 15. Find each technology’s globally optimal scale on [0,1], and current and bad-state consumption for optimal A. Explain why baseline positive marginal value does not imply full implementation.
  6. For deterministic marginal valuation set β=1/1.01, annual growth g=0.01 and curvature η=2. Derive the gross consumption discount rate and present value of a guaranteed marginal benefit of 100 in year 30. Compare with current marginal cost 40. Explain which assumptions fail if protection pays especially in poor states.
  7. Solve the extraction model at S=1/5 and S=25, including unused stock and λ. Verify the inactive-date inequality in the small-stock case. Must an exhaustible resource always be exhausted?
  8. Add a tax of one per extracted unit at both dates in case 4, refunded to consumers at its date of payment. Find extraction, consumer prices, net-of-tax scarcity rents and discounted government receipts. Verify budgets and distinguish a tax-adjusted Hotelling condition from climate optimality.
  9. Repeat the private and social capacity choices of case 5 for capacity costs c=3, c=1 and c=7/4. Give every optimizer when there is a tie. Explain why an emissions charge need not change capacity at every parameter value.
  10. A single emissions pulse at date zero affects stock at dates one and two only; damage is four per unit of stock at both dates, β=9/10 and utility is quasilinear. Derive its date-zero marginal damage for ρ=1/2 and ρ=1. Explain the timing exponent and the limits of interpreting these numbers as a real social cost of carbon.
Complete solutions

1. A tight cap and a saturated emitter

Total abatement must be ten. Substitute a₂=10−a₁ with a₁∈[4,6]. The derivative of a₁²/2+(10−a₁)² is 3a₁−20, negative throughout this interval, so the unique minimum is a₁=6,a₂=4. The interior second emitter sets permit price eight; emitter 1 has marginal cost six below eight and is at its upper limit, exactly the correct boundary sign. (a₁,a₂,price,cost,damage,receipts)=(6,4,8,34,1,16). Total loss 35 exceeds the unconstrained efficient loss 144/7. The allocation is cost effective conditional on a needlessly tight cap, not welfare optimal.

2. Incidence and compensation

Household 1 receives no rebate, so U₁=60−288/49−432/49−288/49=276/7. Household 2 receives 1152/49, so U₂=60−144/49−720/49+1152/49−288/49=60. Thus (U₁,U₂,minimum compensation)=(276/7,60,18/7). After that transfer, household 1 is at 42 and household 2 at 402/7, above 42. Total surplus is unchanged; compensation is feasible but must actually occur before calling the change a Pareto improvement. Lump-sum transfers fixed independently of actions preserve the abatement incentives.

3. Steep damage

Now ā=(40−2)/6=19/3 and τ=4(10−19/3)=44/3. Full-information choices are ā−θ/6: 13/2 and 37/6. Tax choices are ā−θ/2: 41/6 and 35/6. All are between zero and ten; cost intercepts remain positive. (cap,tax,cap regret,tax regret)=(19/3,44/3,1/12,1/3). The tax has four times the expected regret. The cap wins because d/k=2 and the squared emissions error is now sufficiently costly, not because quantities are intrinsically preferable.

4. Damage uncertainty is a different experiment

At mean damage slope two, ā=(20−2)/4=9/2 and τ=2(10−9/2)=11. The firm’s cost is certain, so its tax response is (11−2)/2=9/2 in both damage states; the cap induces exactly the same action. Mean cost plus damage at that action is 119/2. Full-information choices are 8/3 and 28/5. Quadratic loss gaps are (3/2)(9/2−8/3)²=121/24 and (5/2)(9/2−28/5)²=121/40. Therefore (abatement,tax,expected cost,expected regret)=(9/2,11,119/2,121/30). Full-information expected cost is 832/15. Because neither instrument’s private response depends on d, the behavioral flexibility driving the cost-shock ranking is absent.

5. An interior protection scale

For A the derivative is −15/(100−15x)+9/(50+20x). Multiplication by positive denominators gives 150−435x, so its sole zero is 10/29. The second derivative is strictly negative and endpoint derivatives bracket zero, proving the unique global optimum. For B, the numerator is −1350−435x, always negative, so xB=0. (xA,xB,C₀,Cbad)=(10/29,0,2750/29,1650/29). Baseline marginal benefit 18 exceeds cost 15, so beginning A is worthwhile; marginal utility changes along the project make its later units less attractive. A marginal criterion must be updated, or the full concave objective solved.

6. The horizon compounds assumptions

R=(1.01)²/(1/1.01)=1.01³=1.030301. Hence PV=100/R³⁰=100/(1.01)⁹⁰, giving (R,PV)=(1.030301,40.8391185151344). Relative to cost 40 the stipulated marginal project is favorable by about 0.839119 consumption units. This is a marginal benefit comparison along an assumed path, not a finite-project welfare calculation or a market forecast. If payoffs concentrate in poor states, m and X covary; E[mX] replaces deterministic discounting. β and η also embody the selected welfare criterion, while g is a consumption assumption; none is an estimated climate response.

7. Scarce and abundant deposits

At S=1/5, q₀=1/5,q₁=0 and λ=49/5. The inactive future marginal net benefit has present value (4/5)12=48/5, below λ=49/5; equivalently 12<(5/4)λ=49/4. Thus moving a small unit to the future loses value. At S=25 the unconstrained net-benefit maxima are q₀=10,q₁=12, leaving three unused with λ=0. (small q₀,small q₁,small λ,large q₀,large q₁,unused)=(1/5,0,49/5,10,12,3). Positive marginal benefit from further extraction is absent once net marginal benefits reach zero. Physical exhaustibility alone does not require economic exhaustion.

8. Tax-adjusted rents

The owner’s private unit cost becomes three. The interior equal-rent condition is 9−q₀=(4/5)(11−q₁), with q₀+q₁=8. Thus (q₀,q₁,p₀,p₁,net rent₀,net rent₁,PV receipts)=(11/3,13/3,25/3,29/3,16/3,20/3,107/15). Net rents grow at 5/4. At each date consumers pay pq and receive rebate q; the owner receives (p−3)q; adding numeraire holdings gives 100−pq+q+(p−3)q=100−2q, exactly real extraction resources. Government receives and returns q. Receipts discounted at β are 11/3+(4/5)(13/3)=107/15. Efficiency would require the tax to equal the relevant marginal external harm under a specified damage model. The arithmetic and Hotelling condition do not establish that fact.

9. Capacity regions and ties

Private thresholds are h/4=5/4 and 3h/4=15/4; social thresholds are 7/4 and 21/4. At c=3 both choose ten. At c=1 both choose twenty. At c=7/4 the private choice is uniquely ten, while every social K between ten and twenty minimizes cost because the second segment is flat. (private at3,social at3,private at1,social at1,private at7/4,social lower,social upper)=(10,10,20,20,10,10,20). Convex segment slopes prove completeness of these sets. An incentive change can alter costs and rents while the minimizing capacity remains at the same kink. Observing unchanged capacity alone therefore does not identify zero welfare effect or zero emissions incentive.

10. A finite stock pulse

The pulse first enters S₁ with coefficient one and reaches S₂ with coefficient ρ; it does not enter S₀. Its discounted marginal damage is 4β+4ρβ². Therefore (damage atρhalf,damage atρone)=(261/50,171/25), or 5.22 and 6.84. Differentiating the recurrence explains the exponent j−1 for a date-zero pulse. The comparison holds damage, discounting and the two-date horizon fixed. Actual evaluation needs empirically defensible stock dynamics, horizons, marginal damages, uncertainty and welfare weights. These illustrative values provide none of that calibration; they only verify timing and units.

Teach-back, retention and research discipline

Teach-back. In five minutes explain why equal marginal abatement costs need not mean the emissions cap is optimal; why a tax receipt is not a resource benefit; why a safe discount rate can undervalue protection in a bad state; and why Hotelling concerns net rent. Use one boundary condition in each explanation. A successful explanation names the objective, the decision-maker, the relevant information and the payment counterparty. Repeating a formula without these distinctions is insufficient.

Delayed retention. A week later, without the solutions, rederive the squared-loss instrument comparison, the three extraction regimes and the renewable-capacity correspondence. Then change one assumption: let tax refunds depend on output, protection pay in richer states, or capacity costs sit exactly on a threshold. State which proof step changes before recalculating. Check the result against Exercises 2, 5 and 9, and redo any failed derivation from its feasible set.

For a research extension, propose an emissions-pricing evaluation with measured quantities, price incidence and household rebates. State the treatment and comparison units, policy anticipation, concurrent reforms, spillovers and selection into exposure; preregister a falsifiable mechanism prediction. A before-and-after fall in emissions could reflect recession or imported production rather than the policy. A persuasive welfare claim additionally needs resource costs, displaced emissions, damage estimates and distributional weights. Report separately what is identified, calibrated or ethically chosen. The planned health, education and demographic chapter applies related incentive and welfare distinctions to human outcomes.

Sources and further study

  • MIT 15.023J Global Climate Change: instrument choice lecture (Spring 2008, lec15.pdf) — Conceptual context for cost effectiveness and cost-uncertainty instrument comparison; original proof and numerical economy in chapter.
  • Hunt Allcott, Natural Resource Economics, MIT 14.42 Lecture Plan 16 (21 April 2011) — Finite resource allocation, scarcity multipliers and competitive net-rent condition; own boundary-complete derivation.
  • Thomas J. Sargent and John Stachurski, Asset Pricing: Finite State Models — Finite-state consumption discounting, equity valuation and fundamental matrix context; all examples and computations here are original.
